paper_a.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding

paper_b.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training

metadata.description: BERT and GPT are concurrent, competing frameworks for the same problem: pre-train a Transformer on unlabeled text and fine-tune on downstream NLP tasks. They differ in architectural choice (bidirectional Transformer encoder vs. left-to-right Transformer decoder) and pre-training objective (MLM + NSP vs. autoregressive LM). Both share the two-stage pre-train/fine-tune framework, the same evaluation suite (GLUE), the same Transformer backbone, and overlapping fine-tuning machinery; BERT explicitly contrasts itself with GPT and reports head-to-head numbers.

matches.explanation: Both papers state the same problem: pre-train language representations on a large unlabeled corpus and adapt them with minimal task-specific change to a wide range of supervised downstream NLP tasks (NLI, QA, similarity, classification). BERT phrases it as 'deep bidirectional language representation pre-training' while GPT calls it 'semi-supervised language understanding', but the goal and the downstream task family are identical.

Both papers define the two-stage pre-train/fine-tune framework: stage 1 is unsupervised LM-style pre-training on raw text, stage 2 initializes a task model from the pre-trained parameters and fine-tunes end-to-end with a single new output layer. BERT abstracts this as a definition (DP224.5); GPT folds it into the master algorithm (AP225.1). The match is cross-type (definition vs. algorithm) but corresponds to the same conceptual contribution that this paradigm exists and works across many tasks.

Both define the model backbone as a multi-layer Transformer with multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward layers. BERT uses a bidirectional Transformer ENCODER (no causal mask), reported at L=12, H=768, A=12 (BASE) and L=24, H=1024, A=16 (LARGE). GPT uses a Transformer DECODER (causal, masked self-attention) at L=12, H=768, A=12. The 'analogous' tag flags the encoder-vs-decoder (bidirectional vs. left-to-right) distinction that is the core architectural difference of the pair. Note GPT cites the Transformer (DP225.3 origin=external); BERT also cites it (DP224.8) but additionally defines its own bidirectional instantiation (DP224.1).

Both nodes are external citations of Vaswani et al. 2017 'Attention Is All You Need' (DP224.8 and DP225.3 both have origin=external with that citation). This is a shared dependency on prior work — informative about provenance but, per the prompt, carries no information about the pair-level relationship beyond confirming a common backbone.

These are the two papers' pre-training objectives, and they are the central theoretical difference of the pair. BERT's Masked LM (DP224.3) randomly masks 15% of tokens (80/10/10 mask/random/keep) and predicts the originals from a bidirectional context. GPT's autoregressive LM (EP225.1) maximizes $\sum_i \log P(u_i \mid u_{i-k}, \dots, u_{i-1}; \Theta)$ — strictly left-to-right. Both are unsupervised, token-level, cross-entropy objectives parameterized by a Transformer; both serve the same role (the pre-training signal) — hence 'analogous'. BERT's RP224.1 explicitly motivates MLM by arguing that naive bidirectionalization of a left-to-right LM (i.e., GPT's objective) is impossible, so this pair is the single most important alignment in the file.

Next Sentence Prediction is a BERT-specific second pre-training task (binary IsNext/NotNext on the [CLS] vector). GPT has no inter-sentence pre-training objective; its only pre-training signal is the token-level autoregressive LM. BERT's own ablation (ExP224.7) shows NSP matters for QNLI/MNLI/SQuAD.

BERT's input representation (token + segment + position embeddings, [CLS]/[SEP] specials) is a paper-original design tied to MLM/NSP and to the bidirectional encoder reading two segments in one sequence. GPT uses learned token + position embeddings only, plus task-specific delimiter $ and start/end tokens introduced at fine-tuning time (handled in AP225.2 / ASP225.2). Segment embeddings and the [CLS]-as-classifier convention are BERT-specific.

Both are the unsupervised pre-training algorithms. BERT's AP224.1 trains a bidirectional Transformer on BooksCorpus + Wikipedia with MLM + NSP for 1M steps (Adam, lr 1e-4). GPT's ASP225.1 trains a 12-layer Transformer decoder on BooksCorpus with the autoregressive LM (Adam via AP225.3, max lr 2.5e-4, cosine schedule). Same role (the pre-training stage) but with different objectives, different corpora (BERT adds Wikipedia), and different optimizer schedules — hence 'analogous'. Granularity differs: BERT promotes pre-training to a top-level algorithm, GPT keeps it as an algorithm_step inside AP225.1; this match crosses Level-1/Level-2 (allowed under L2 rule 2 because the boundary is genuinely paper-specific).

Both are the fine-tuning procedures. BERT's AP224.2 initializes from pre-trained parameters, swaps in a task-specific head, packs single or paired inputs, and back-propagates the task loss through all parameters with Adam (sweeping batch/lr/epochs). GPT's ASP225.3 adds a linear head $W_y$ and maximizes the combined objective $L_3 = L_2 + \lambda L_1$ on the labeled data. Two key differences: (i) GPT keeps the auxiliary LM loss during fine-tuning, BERT does not; (ii) BERT fine-tunes on the bidirectional [CLS] vector while GPT reads out the final-token hidden state of a causal model. Cross-level match (L1 vs L2) is justified by the same granularity asymmetry as AP224.1 ↔ ASP225.1.

Both papers define the supervised classification head as a softmax over a final-layer hidden state times new task-specific weights. BERT (EP224.1): $\mathcal{L} = -\log\,\mathrm{softmax}(C W^\top)$ on the [CLS] hidden $C$. GPT (EP225.3, EP225.4): $P(y \mid x) = \mathrm{softmax}(h_l^m W_y)$ on the final-token hidden, with the dataset-level loss $L_2 = \sum \log P$. The functional form is the same up to which token's hidden vector is used — a direct consequence of the bidirectional vs. left-to-right architecture (BERT can use a dedicated [CLS] position; GPT must use the last token of the causal sequence).

GPT's combined fine-tuning objective $L_3 = L_2 + \lambda L_1$ — keeping the language-modeling auxiliary loss as a regularizer during fine-tuning — has no BERT counterpart. BERT discards the pre-training objective at fine-tuning time entirely. GPT's RP225.1 reports that this auxiliary loss helps on larger datasets (NLI, QQP) but not smaller ones.

GPT's 'task-specific input transformations' (a unified traversal-style scheme using delimiter $ and start/end tokens to convert structured inputs — entailment pairs, similarity pairs, document/question/answers — into a single token sequence) is GPT's signature contribution and has no BERT analogue. BERT instead packs paired inputs with [CLS] and [SEP] (handled inside ASP224.7), and uses a different recipe per task family (single, pair, span, multi-choice). The two papers solve the same engineering problem (how to feed structured tasks to a sequence model) with substantially different conventions.

Composite L2-vs-L2 match for the 'pack structured task input' substep (allowed because both sides are children of paired L1 algorithms BERT's AP224.2 and GPT's AP225.2 / AP225.1, which are themselves matched above). BERT's ASP224.7 packs single or paired inputs with [CLS]/[SEP] using segment embeddings A/B. GPT's ASP225.5/6/7 instead build per-task token sequences using delimiter $ and start/end tokens, with task-specific tricks (e.g. sum two orderings for similarity, score each candidate independently for QA). Same role (input packing), different convention.

BERT's SQuAD span-prediction machinery — the start/end vector formulation $S, E \in \mathbb{R}^H$ (AP224.3), the start probability $P_i = \frac{e^{S\cdot T_i}}{\sum_j e^{S\cdot T_j}}$ (EP224.2), and the SQuAD 2.0 no-answer thresholding rule using $s_{\text{null}} = S\cdot C + E\cdot C$ (EP224.3) — has no GPT counterpart. GPT does not evaluate on SQuAD and does not introduce span-prediction heads.

Both papers cite a subword tokenizer as an external dependency and use it to build their input vocabulary. BERT uses WordPiece (DP224.6, Wu et al. 2016) with 30k vocab; GPT uses Byte-Pair Encoding (DP225.4, Sennrich et al. 2015) with 40k merges. Same role (subword tokenization for the pre-training corpus), different specific algorithm — hence 'analogous'. Both nodes are origin=external.

GPT explicitly cites GELU (Hendrycks & Gimpel 2016) as its activation. BERT also uses GELU (mentioned in passing inside AP224.1's input list as 'gelu activation') but does not lift it to its own definition node. We omit a definition-level match; if anything BERT's GELU usage is implicit. Marked 'none' on the BERT side to flag this asymmetry, with medium confidence because BERT does in fact use the same activation — only the extraction granularity differs.

GPT promotes Adam (with linear warmup + cosine decay, max lr 2.5e-4) to its own algorithm node with origin=external. BERT also uses Adam (with warmup + linear decay, lr 1e-4) but only mentions it in the input list of AP224.1. This is a shared external dependency that the two extractions chose to surface at different granularities. Per the origin-aware filtering rule, external↔external matches carry no signal about the pair relationship; we record GPT's side as 'none' to keep the alignment compact rather than emit a contentless external↔external entry.

BERT cites the classical Cloze task (Taylor 1953) as the inspiration for MLM. GPT, whose objective is left-to-right autoregression, has no analogue — its lineage runs through LSTM language models rather than fill-in-the-blank tasks. External-origin node, included as 'none' only because it is conceptually load-bearing for BERT's central design choice.

BERT's remark that standard bidirectional conditioning fails (each word would 'see itself' through multiple layers) is the core motivation distinguishing MLM from a left-to-right LM. GPT, being left-to-right by design, has no parallel concern — making this remark a clean BERT-only contribution that directly explains why the two papers diverge architecturally.

BERT's Appendix B remark explicitly contrasts BERT vs OpenAI GPT vs ELMo. This is a paper-original 'sibling comparison' from BERT's side; the GPT paper, written months earlier, cannot reciprocate. ExP224.3 and ExP224.6 also report BERT_LARGE beating GPT by 7.7 points on GLUE and 8.3% on SWAG, so this is the textual hook for the head-to-head comparison underlying the entire pair.

BERT's pre-train/fine-tune mismatch remark (the [MASK] token never appears at fine-tuning) is specific to MLM. GPT has no such mismatch because its pre-training objective (next-token prediction) and its fine-tuning input format share the same token distribution. Listed as 'none' to mark this as a BERT-only design issue.

BERT's remark on the cheap cost of fine-tuning (≤1 hour on a single TPU) is a reproducibility note. GPT does not state an analogous bound, though its fine-tuning is similarly cheap. Marked 'none' for completeness; low confidence because the absence is plausibly an extraction artifact rather than a real difference.

BERT's 90/10 sequence-length schedule (length 128 for 90% of steps, 512 for 10%) is a BERT-specific compute-saving trick tied to its bidirectional attention (quadratic in sequence length). GPT trains at fixed sequence length 512 and does not introduce this schedule.

Both papers report a GLUE leaderboard score, and BERT's ExP224.3 explicitly compares to GPT's number: BERT_LARGE 80.5 vs OpenAI GPT 72.8. GPT's ExP225.5 reports overall GLUE 72.8 (vs previous best 68.9). This is the single most direct empirical link between the two papers — the GPT result is literally the baseline BERT beats. 'Analogous' rather than 'exact' because the underlying systems differ; the alignment is at the level of 'same benchmark, head-to-head numbers'.

BERT's pre-training-task ablation (No NSP, LTR & No NSP, +BiLSTM) is a direct empirical comparison with the GPT-style left-to-right objective: the LTR & No NSP variant IS essentially GPT's pre-training recipe applied to BERT's encoder, and BERT shows it loses on every task. This is a paper-original BERT contribution with no GPT counterpart and is a key piece of evidence behind the CF classification.

Both papers run a 'scale matters' ablation: BERT's ExP224.8 varies (L,H,A) and shows monotone gains down to small fine-tuning sets like MRPC; GPT's ExP225.6 varies the number of pre-trained Transformer layers transferred to MultiNLI/RACE and shows monotone gains. Same conceptual experiment (transfer scales with pre-trained model capacity / depth), different operationalization (model size sweep vs. layer-transfer sweep). 'Analogous' with medium confidence — the overlap is at the level of finding rather than method.

BERT's feature-based experiment on CoNLL-2003 NER (freezing BERT activations, feeding them into a randomly-initialized BiLSTM) targets the contrast with ELMo, not GPT. GPT does not run a feature-based variant or evaluate on CoNLL NER.

BERT's number-of-pre-training-steps ablation (1M vs 500k steps, MLM vs LTR convergence) is BERT-specific. GPT does not report a steps-vs-accuracy curve at this granularity. The MLM-vs-LTR convergence comparison inside ExP224.10 again pits BERT's recipe against GPT's; we keep this as a BERT-only ablation rather than a match.
Different masking procedures ablation is specific to MLM and therefore to BERT. GPT has no masking strategy to ablate.

GPT's BooksCorpus pre-training perplexity (18.4) is a GPT-only intrinsic-LM number. BERT pre-trains on BooksCorpus + Wikipedia (so corpus differs) and reports no perplexity (MLM perplexity is not directly comparable to autoregressive perplexity anyway). Same corpus partially overlaps but no comparable metric exists.

GPT reports gains on five NLI benchmarks (MNLI, SNLI, SciTail, QNLI, RTE). BERT also evaluates on MNLI, QNLI, RTE (inside the GLUE umbrella, ExP224.3) but does not enumerate per-NLI-dataset gains as a separate result. Listed as 'none' on the BERT side because there is no equivalent ablation node; the GLUE-vs-GLUE match (ExP224.3 ↔ ExP225.5) already captures the head-to-head signal.
GPT's QA results on RACE and Story Cloze have no BERT counterpart in this extraction; BERT evaluates on SQuAD v1.1 / v2.0 instead (ExP224.4 / ExP224.5).
BERT's SQuAD v1.1 (Test F1 93.2) and SQuAD v2.0 (+5.1 F1, Test F1 83.1) results have no GPT counterpart; GPT does not evaluate on SQuAD. Symmetric to the GPT QA-results 'none' above.
BERT's SWAG result (BERT_LARGE +27.1% over ESIM+ELMo, +8.3% over OpenAI GPT) is a direct BERT-vs-GPT comparison from BERT's side; GPT predates SWAG's heavy use and has no SWAG node here.

GPT's semantic similarity results (MRPC, QQP, STS-B) are inside GLUE and so are subsumed into the ExP224.3 ↔ ExP225.5 GLUE-overall match. GPT separately reports MRPC and QQP gains; BERT folds them into the GLUE table without a separate similarity node. Listed as 'none' on the BERT side for completeness.

GPT's zero-shot heuristic evaluation (using only the generative model with task-shaped probes — log-prob thresholds for CoLA, 'positive vs negative' continuation for SST-2, etc.) is a GPT-original analysis with no BERT counterpart. BERT cannot natively perform autoregressive generation, so these probes are not available. This is genuine GPT-side signal (and a precursor to GPT-2/GPT-3 zero-shot evaluation).

GPT's three-way ablation (no auxiliary LM during fine-tuning; LSTM instead of Transformer; no pre-training at all) has no single BERT counterpart. BERT's closest analogue is ExP224.7 (pre-training-task ablation), but that ablates the OBJECTIVE (MLM vs NSP vs LTR), not the architecture or the auxiliary loss. Listed as 'none' to reflect the asymmetric ablation design.

GPT's remark that the auxiliary LM helps larger datasets (NLI, QQP) but not smaller ones is specific to GPT's L_3 = L_2 + lambda L_1 design (see EP225.5 'none' above) — BERT has no auxiliary loss at fine-tuning.

GPT's justification of BooksCorpus (long contiguous text → long-range conditioning) is a corpus-choice remark. BERT additionally uses Wikipedia and does not surface this argument; instead BERT addresses long-range learning via the 90/10 sequence-length schedule (RP224.5).

GPT's remark that the Transformer's structured attentional memory transfers better than an LSTM's is a Transformer-vs-LSTM motivation; BERT, which already takes the Transformer for granted, does not state an analogous defense (it only contrasts with ELMo's BiLSTM in RP224.3, and even there the focus is bidirectionality, not the Transformer-vs-LSTM axis).

GLUE benchmark (Wang et al. 2018) is cited by both papers as the umbrella evaluation, but the GPT JSON does not surface GLUE as its own problem node — GLUE results are folded into ExP225.5. We capture the empirical link at ExP224.3 ↔ ExP225.5 above and skip the external↔(missing-external) match here per the origin-aware filtering rule. (External-origin node included as 'none' on the BERT side only because the prompt requires every Level-1 node to appear; in the next pass it could be omitted.)

BERT's external-origin downstream-task definitions (SQuAD v1.1, SQuAD v2.0, SWAG, CoNLL-2003 NER) have no matching GPT-side problem nodes — GPT evaluates on a different downstream-task slate (RACE, Story Cloze, NLI suite, semantic similarity, classification). Grouped into one 'none' entry to keep the alignment compact, all four are origin=external.

BERT's two illustrative input examples — the 'my dog is hairy' MLM masking example (ExP224.1) and the IsNext/NotNext NSP pair example (ExP224.2) — illustrate BERT-specific objectives (MLM and NSP) and have no GPT counterpart. Listed for completeness; auxiliary-type 'example' nodes are not strictly required to receive 'none' entries (per the compactness rule), but these two are tightly tied to the two BERT objectives that distinguish the pair.

GPT defines 'unsupervised token corpus' $\mathcal{U} = \{u_1,\dots,u_n\}$ as a separate node — the input to the language-modeling objective. BERT does not lift the unlabeled corpus to a definition node; it appears only inside AP224.1's input list ('BooksCorpus 800M words + English Wikipedia 2,500M words'). Same conceptual object (unlabeled pre-training corpus) but different extraction granularity, so listed as 'none' with medium confidence.

GPT defines 'labeled target dataset' $\mathcal{C} = \{(x^1,\dots,x^m, y)\}$ as a separate node. BERT does not surface the labeled-task dataset as its own definition; it is implicit in AP224.2's input list. Same role (the supervised fine-tuning data) but BERT keeps it implicit.

GPT writes out the Transformer forward pass equationally: $h_0 = U W_e + W_p$, $h_l = \mathrm{transformer\_block}(h_{l-1})$, $P(u) = \mathrm{softmax}(h_n W_e^T)$ (note tied input/output embedding matrix $W_e$). BERT does not write out the encoder forward pass as an equation node — the architecture is summarized at definition level (DP224.1) and the masked-LM and NSP heads are surfaced as a definition (DP224.3) and a loss equation (EP224.1) instead. Cross-extraction granularity mismatch; weighted as 'none' on the BERT side rather than forcing a low-confidence cross-type match.
